meta.notice: This corpus demonstrates a mechanism; it is not an authoritative fact-checking result. It contains common public claims with links to authoritative sources. Every snippet is a human-written English paraphrase, not a verbatim quotation; click the source to check the original text. Where sources differ in wording, the tool displays the difference without adjudicating and takes no position on the topic.

field_meanings.stance: supports = this source supports the claim; refutes = this source refutes it; contextual = background only; conflicting = sources differ in wording
field_meanings.card_id: unique evidence-card identifier used for citation
field_meanings.snippet: human-written paraphrase; click url to verify the original
field_meanings.conflict_group: group of cards whose sources differ in wording; a hit forces refusal and shows both sides
field_meanings.exclude_if: scope guard: a general card yields to a more specific claim

evidence_cards.claim: Getting a flu vaccine gives you the flu
evidence_cards.source_name: WHO · Five myths about the flu vaccine
evidence_cards.snippet: WHO: injected seasonal flu vaccines contain no live virus and cannot cause influenza; mild soreness is common, but the vaccine does not give you the flu.

evidence_cards.claim: Antibiotics can treat a common cold or flu
evidence_cards.snippet: CDC: colds and flu are viral illnesses; antibiotics treat bacterial infections and do not work on viruses.

evidence_cards.claim: 5G phone signals spread the coronavirus
evidence_cards.snippet: WHO: viruses cannot travel on radio waves or mobile networks; COVID-19 spreads through respiratory droplets.

evidence_cards.claim: The Earth is round
evidence_cards.snippet: NASA: people have known Earth is round for more than two thousand years; the curved shadow in lunar eclipses, satellite measurements and space photographs all support this.

evidence_cards.claim: A certain water purifier can cure diabetes
evidence_cards.snippet: No source in this corpus supports such a product claim. Included as an example of an unsupported claim that must trigger refusal.

evidence_cards.claim: Getting the flu after vaccination proves the vaccine is completely ineffective
evidence_cards.source_name: WHO · Five myths about the flu vaccine
evidence_cards.snippet: WHO: vaccination reduces the risk of severe disease; breakthrough infections occur because immunity wanes and circulating strains change, not because the vaccine is useless.

evidence_cards.claim: The flu vaccine contains live virus and causes infection
evidence_cards.source_name: WHO · Seven things to know about influenza vaccination
evidence_cards.snippet: WHO: the injected flu vaccine contains no live virus. The nasal-spray form uses weakened virus that does not cause flu in healthy people.

evidence_cards.claim: The flu vaccine needs to be taken every year
evidence_cards.source_name: WHO · Seven things to know about influenza vaccination
evidence_cards.snippet: WHO: antibody levels decline over time and flu strains change, so annual vaccination is recommended.

evidence_cards.claim: Pregnant women cannot receive the flu vaccine
evidence_cards.source_name: WHO · Five myths about the flu vaccine
evidence_cards.snippet: WHO: flu vaccination is safe and recommended during pregnancy and protects both mother and baby.

evidence_cards.claim: The flu vaccine causes severe side effects
evidence_cards.source_name: WHO · Five myths about the flu vaccine
evidence_cards.snippet: WHO: typical side effects are mild and short-lived; severe reactions are very rare.

evidence_cards.claim: Flu is not serious, so vaccination is unnecessary
evidence_cards.source_name: WHO · Five myths about the flu vaccine
evidence_cards.snippet: WHO: influenza can cause severe disease and death, especially in high-risk groups; vaccination is the best available prevention.

evidence_cards.claim: Antibiotics can cure COVID-19
evidence_cards.snippet: WHO: COVID-19 is viral; antibiotics do not work on viruses and are used only for secondary bacterial infections.

evidence_cards.claim: A common cold can resolve on its own
evidence_cards.source_name: US CDC · Treating the common cold
evidence_cards.snippet: CDC: most people recover from a common cold without specific treatment in about one to two weeks.

evidence_cards.claim: Antibiotic resistance means the body becomes resistant to antibiotics
evidence_cards.snippet: CDC and WHO: bacteria become resistant to antibiotics; the human body does not.

evidence_cards.claim: Taking antibiotics helps people return to work faster
evidence_cards.source_name: US CDC Stacks · Antibiotic awareness poster
evidence_cards.snippet: CDC: for viral colds antibiotics provide no benefit and can cause harm; they do not speed recovery.

evidence_cards.claim: Antibiotics are effective against bacterial infections
evidence_cards.snippet: CDC: antibiotics are used to treat infections caused by bacteria, not viruses.

evidence_cards.claim: Alcohol-based hand sanitizer creates antibiotic resistance
evidence_cards.snippet: WHO: pathogens do not appear to develop resistance to alcohol-based hand rubs, unlike antibiotics.

evidence_cards.claim: Wearing a medical mask causes carbon-dioxide poisoning
evidence_cards.snippet: WHO: masks do not cause CO2 poisoning; oxygen and carbon dioxide pass through the mask material.

evidence_cards.claim: Swimming spreads the coronavirus through pool water
evidence_cards.snippet: WHO: the virus is not spread through properly chlorinated swimming-pool water.

evidence_cards.claim: Shoes are a high-probability route for coronavirus transmission
evidence_cards.snippet: WHO mythbusters: the risk of infection from shoes is low; routine cleaning is sufficient.

evidence_cards.claim: Vitamin supplements can cure COVID-19
evidence_cards.snippet: WHO: there is no evidence that vitamin or mineral supplements cure COVID-19; they are not a treatment.

evidence_cards.claim: Wearing gloves can replace hand washing
evidence_cards.snippet: WHO: gloves can transfer germs between surfaces and contaminate hands when removed; hand cleaning remains essential.

evidence_cards.claim: COVID-19 is caused by bacteria
evidence_cards.snippet: WHO: COVID-19 is caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, not by bacteria.

evidence_cards.claim: Frequent hand washing reduces viral transmission
evidence_cards.snippet: WHO: cleaning hands is one of the key measures for preventing infection.

evidence_cards.claim: The Earth is a perfect sphere
evidence_cards.source_name: NASA Earthdata · Fifty years of satellite laser ranging
evidence_cards.snippet: NASA: Earth is an oblate spheroid, slightly flattened at the poles and bulging at the equator, not a perfect sphere.

evidence_cards.claim: High-altitude balloon photos show the Earth's curvature
evidence_cards.source_name: NASA · 90 Years of Our Changing Views of Earth
evidence_cards.snippet: NASA: high-altitude photographs have shown Earth's curved horizon since the early days of ballooning.

evidence_cards.claim: During a lunar eclipse, Earth's shadow on the Moon is curved
evidence_cards.snippet: NASA: the curved shadow on the Moon during a lunar eclipse is one of the oldest observations supporting a round Earth.

evidence_cards.claim: Planets are cube-shaped
evidence_cards.snippet: NASA: gravity pulls large bodies into roughly spherical shapes; no known planet is cube-shaped.

evidence_cards.claim: Saturn is the roundest planet in the solar system
evidence_cards.snippet: NASA: Saturn is strongly oblate because of rapid rotation, so it is not the roundest planet.

evidence_cards.claim: Earth's rotation makes the poles slightly flattened
evidence_cards.source_name: NASA Earthdata · Fifty years of satellite laser ranging
evidence_cards.snippet: NASA: rotation produces a slight equatorial bulge and polar flattening; Earth is an oblate spheroid.

evidence_cards.claim: Microwave ovens make food radioactive
evidence_cards.snippet: US FDA: microwaves are non-ionizing radiation; they heat food but leave no residual radiation.

evidence_cards.claim: Microwave cooking destroys more nutrients than conventional cooking
evidence_cards.snippet: USDA and FDA: nutrient retention depends mainly on cooking time and temperature; microwaving often preserves nutrients well.

evidence_cards.claim: Microwaves heat food from the inside out
evidence_cards.source_name: US USDA FSIS · Microwave cooking and food safety
evidence_cards.snippet: USDA FSIS: microwaves penetrate only a few centimetres; heat then spreads by conduction, so the centre may stay cold.

evidence_cards.claim: An intact microwave oven leaks microwaves
evidence_cards.snippet: US FDA: a properly functioning oven is designed to contain microwaves and must meet strict leakage limits.

evidence_cards.claim: Microwaves are non-ionizing radiation
evidence_cards.snippet: US FDA: microwave energy is non-ionizing and cannot break chemical bonds or make food radioactive.

evidence_cards.claim: Humans use only ten percent of their brains
evidence_cards.source_name: China Digital Science & Technology Museum · Science Pictorial
evidence_cards.snippet: CDSTM: brain imaging shows the whole brain stays active even when a person is not thinking; no region is permanently idle, so the 10% figure is a myth.

evidence_cards.claim: The brain remains active while resting
evidence_cards.source_name: China Digital Science & Technology Museum · Science Pictorial
evidence_cards.snippet: CDSTM: even when a subject is thinking about nothing, the entire brain keeps working; resting does not mean idle.

evidence_cards.claim: Food left at room temperature for over two hours is still safe
evidence_cards.source_name: US USDA · The two-hour food safety rule
evidence_cards.snippet: USDA: perishable food left in the temperature danger zone for more than two hours should be discarded (one hour above 32 C).

evidence_cards.claim: Meat colour is a reliable indicator of doneness
evidence_cards.source_name: US USDA · The two-hour food safety rule
evidence_cards.snippet: USDA: colour is not a reliable indicator of a safe internal temperature; use a food thermometer.

evidence_cards.claim: Frozen food can be thawed on the counter at room temperature
evidence_cards.source_name: US USDA · The two-hour food safety rule
evidence_cards.snippet: USDA: thaw in the refrigerator, in cold water or in the microwave, never on the counter.

evidence_cards.claim: Vaccines overwhelm an infant's immune system
evidence_cards.snippet: CDC: vaccines expose the immune system to small amounts of antigen, far less than infants encounter every day.

evidence_cards.claim: Delaying vaccination is safer for children
evidence_cards.snippet: CDC: the recommended schedule protects children earlier; delay leaves them vulnerable to disease.

evidence_cards.claim: Splitting the MMR vaccine into three separate shots works better
evidence_cards.snippet: CDC: separate shots would require more visits and provide no safety or effectiveness advantage.

evidence_cards.claim: One flu shot gives lifelong protection
evidence_cards.source_name: WHO · Seven things to know about influenza vaccination
evidence_cards.snippet: WHO: circulating strains change and immunity wanes, so annual vaccination is needed.

evidence_cards.claim: Swimming can give you COVID-19
evidence_cards.snippet: WHO: the virus does not spread through properly chlorinated swimming pools.

evidence_cards.claim: Microwaved food is less nutritious than food cooked other ways
evidence_cards.snippet: FDA: nutrient loss is driven mainly by cooking time and temperature, not by microwave cooking itself.

evidence_cards.claim: Food left on the table for three hours is still fine
evidence_cards.source_name: US USDA · The two-hour food safety rule
evidence_cards.snippet: USDA: perishable food left out for three hours is in the bacterial danger zone and should be discarded.

evidence_cards.claim: You can tell if meat is cooked by its colour
evidence_cards.source_name: US USDA · The two-hour food safety rule
evidence_cards.snippet: USDA: only a food thermometer can confirm a safe internal temperature; colour is unreliable.

evidence_cards.claim: The Earth is a sphere
evidence_cards.snippet: NASA: independent lines of evidence show Earth is roughly spherical, with slight polar flattening.

evidence_cards.claim: People use only 10% of their brains
evidence_cards.source_name: China Digital Science & Technology Museum · Science Pictorial
evidence_cards.snippet: CDSTM, citing the Science Pictorial: the brain runs on about 20% of the body's energy at rest, which makes 'only 10% is used' biologically implausible.

evidence_cards.claim: Wearing gloves is more reliable than washing hands
evidence_cards.snippet: WHO: hand cleaning remains the key measure; gloves can spread contamination when removed.

evidence_cards.claim: Delaying vaccination is safer
evidence_cards.snippet: CDC: the recommended schedule is designed for timely protection; delay increases risk.

evidence_cards.claim: Vaccines cause autism
evidence_cards.snippet: CDC MMR safety page: multiple well-designed studies found no association between MMR vaccine and autism. This card is part of a real source-wording discrepancy group.

evidence_cards.claim: Vaccines cause autism
evidence_cards.source_name: US CDC · Autism and vaccines (current page)
evidence_cards.snippet: CDC current page: wording was updated under a data-quality process and differs from the safety page and archived material. The tool shows the difference and takes no position on the topic.

evidence_cards.claim: Eating carrots gives you extraordinary night vision
evidence_cards.source_name: US NIH National Eye Institute · How to Feast for Your Eyes
evidence_cards.snippet: NIH National Eye Institute: no amount of carrots, liver or bilberries gives owl-like night vision; carrots supply vitamin A needed for eye health.

evidence_cards.claim: Eating carrots supports eye health
evidence_cards.source_name: US NIH National Eye Institute · How to Feast for Your Eyes
evidence_cards.snippet: NIH NEI: carrots are rich in vitamin A, which is needed for eye health; a balanced diet supplies the vitamin A most people need.

evidence_cards.claim: MSG is harmful to health
evidence_cards.source_name: US FDA · Questions and Answers on Monosodium glutamate (MSG)
evidence_cards.snippet: FDA: monosodium glutamate is 'generally recognized as safe'; controlled studies could not consistently trigger reactions in self-described sensitive people.

evidence_cards.claim: Eating sugar makes cancer worse
evidence_cards.source_name: US National Cancer Institute · Common Cancer Myths and Misconceptions
evidence_cards.snippet: US NCI: although cancer cells consume more glucose, no studies show that eating sugar worsens cancer or that cutting sugar shrinks tumours.

evidence_cards.claim: Cancer is contagious between people
evidence_cards.source_name: US National Cancer Institute · Common Cancer Myths and Misconceptions
evidence_cards.snippet: US NCI: cancer is generally not contagious; aside from rare transplant transmission, cancer-causing viruses or bacteria can spread but the cancer itself cannot.

evidence_cards.claim: Mobile-phone radiation causes cancer
evidence_cards.source_name: US National Cancer Institute · Common Cancer Myths and Misconceptions
evidence_cards.snippet: US NCI: the best studies to date show mobile phones do not cause cancer; they emit low-frequency energy that does not damage genes.

evidence_cards.claim: Power lines cause cancer
evidence_cards.source_name: US National Cancer Institute · Common Cancer Myths and Misconceptions
evidence_cards.snippet: US NCI: the best available studies show no cancer risk; electric fields are easily shielded and magnetic fields are low-frequency and non-genotoxic.

evidence_cards.claim: A positive attitude determines whether you get cancer
evidence_cards.source_name: US National Cancer Institute · Common Cancer Myths and Misconceptions
evidence_cards.snippet: US NCI: there is no convincing scientific evidence linking a person's attitude to cancer risk or survival.

evidence_cards.claim: Cancer surgery spreads cancer cells
evidence_cards.source_name: US National Cancer Institute · Common Cancer Myths and Misconceptions
evidence_cards.snippet: US NCI: the chance is extremely low; surgeons use separate instruments and specific procedures to prevent spread.

evidence_cards.claim: An alkaline diet can cure cancer
evidence_cards.source_name: US National Cancer Institute · Alkaline diet entry
evidence_cards.snippet: US NCI: there is no proof that an alkaline diet can slow, cure or prevent the return of cancer.

evidence_cards.claim: Touching a shared hand-sanitizer bottle gives you COVID-19
evidence_cards.snippet: WHO mythbusters: once hands are sanitized, germs on the bottle are removed; shared sanitizer use lowers overall risk.

evidence_cards.claim: Normal use of alcohol hand sanitizer causes alcohol poisoning
evidence_cards.snippet: WHO: little alcohol is absorbed through the skin; accidental swallowing and intoxication are described only in rare cases.

evidence_cards.claim: The Earth is flat
evidence_cards.snippet: NASA: satellite imagery, lunar eclipses, circumnavigation and gravity all show that Earth is roughly spherical, not flat.

evidence_cards.claim: Microwaved food has radiation
evidence_cards.snippet: US FDA: microwave energy is non-ionizing and heats food without making it radioactive; no residual radiation remains in the food.

evidence_cards.claim: Vitamin C prevents the common cold
evidence_cards.source_name: US NIH NCCIH · Natural products for flu and colds
evidence_cards.snippet: NCCIH: vitamin C does not prevent colds; a 2013 review found that taking it regularly did not reduce the likelihood of catching one.

evidence_cards.claim: Vitamin C cures a cold once you already have it
evidence_cards.source_name: US NIH NCCIH · Natural products for flu and colds
evidence_cards.snippet: NCCIH: vitamin C only slightly reduces the length and severity of a cold; in studies where people took it after symptoms began, it did not improve them.

evidence_cards.claim: Coffee causes cancer
evidence_cards.source_name: US NCI · Diet and cancer risk
evidence_cards.snippet: US NCI: with few exceptions, studies of human populations have not shown definitively that any dietary component, coffee included among the foods studied, causes cancer.

evidence_cards.claim: Taking 400 mcg of folic acid daily helps prevent neural tube defects
evidence_cards.snippet: CDC: 400 micrograms (mcg) of folic acid daily can help prevent serious birth defects called neural tube defects, and that amount is what the US Public Health Service recommends for anyone who could become pregnant.

evidence_cards.claim: Taking more than 4,000 IU of vitamin D per day exceeds the safe upper limit
evidence_cards.source_name: US NIH ODS · Vitamin D fact sheet
evidence_cards.snippet: NIH ODS: the tolerable upper intake level for vitamin D ranges from 25 to 100 mcg (1,000-4,000 IU) per day depending on age; above that level the risk of toxicity rises.

evidence_cards.claim: Washing hands with soap prevents the spread of respiratory and diarrheal infections
evidence_cards.snippet: CDC: washing hands can keep you healthy and prevent the spread of respiratory and diarrheal infections, and handwashing with soap is one of the best ways to stay healthy.

evidence_cards.claim: Hand sanitizer needs at least 60% alcohol to work
evidence_cards.snippet: CDC: if soap and water are not available, use an alcohol-based hand sanitizer that contains at least 60% alcohol; the label tells you whether it does.

evidence_cards.claim: Antibiotics work on viruses
evidence_cards.snippet: CDC: antibiotics do not treat infections caused by viruses, including colds and flu; they only treat certain bacterial infections.

evidence_cards.claim: Antibiotics have no side effects
evidence_cards.snippet: CDC: taking antibiotics when they are not needed does not help and the side effects can still cause harm; common ones include rash, dizziness, nausea, diarrhea and yeast infections.

evidence_cards.claim: Antibiotic side effects in children are rare
evidence_cards.snippet: CDC: in children, side effects from antibiotics are the most common cause of medication-related emergency department visits.

evidence_cards.claim: Adults need at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity a week
evidence_cards.source_name: CDC · Physical activity guidelines for adults
evidence_cards.snippet: CDC: adults need at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity a week, for example 30 minutes a day on five days.

evidence_cards.claim: Adults need muscle-strengthening activity on two or more days a week
evidence_cards.source_name: CDC · Physical activity guidelines for adults
evidence_cards.snippet: CDC: adults also need at least 2 days of muscle-strengthening activity each week, working all major muscle groups.

evidence_cards.claim: 75 minutes of vigorous activity a week meets the adult guideline
evidence_cards.source_name: CDC · Physical activity guidelines for adults
evidence_cards.snippet: CDC: 150 minutes of moderate activity can be replaced by 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity activity, or an equivalent mix of the two.

evidence_cards.claim: Adults need at least seven hours of sleep a night
evidence_cards.source_name: CDC · How much sleep do I need
evidence_cards.snippet: CDC: adults aged 18 to 60 years are recommended to get 7 or more hours of sleep per night.

evidence_cards.claim: Teenagers need eight to ten hours of sleep per day
evidence_cards.source_name: CDC · How much sleep do I need
evidence_cards.snippet: CDC: teenagers aged 13 to 18 years are recommended to get 8 to 10 hours of sleep per 24 hours.

evidence_cards.claim: Adults should keep sodium intake below 2,300 mg a day
evidence_cards.snippet: CDC: the federal recommendation is less than 2,300 milligrams of sodium daily for teens and adults as part of a healthy eating pattern.

evidence_cards.claim: Too much sodium raises blood pressure
evidence_cards.snippet: CDC: eating too much sodium can increase your blood pressure and your risk for heart disease and stroke.

evidence_cards.claim: Most skin cancers are caused by too much ultraviolet exposure
evidence_cards.snippet: CDC: most skin cancers are caused by too much exposure to ultraviolet rays, which can damage skin cells.

evidence_cards.claim: A broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 15 or higher protects the skin
evidence_cards.snippet: CDC: use a broad-spectrum sunscreen that filters both UVA and UVB rays and has an SPF of 15 or higher before going outside.

evidence_cards.claim: Sunscreen is safe for babies younger than six months
evidence_cards.snippet: CDC: sunscreen is not recommended for babies who are 6 months old or younger; keep infants out of the sun and use protective clothing instead.

evidence_cards.claim: Fluoridated drinking water prevents cavities
evidence_cards.snippet: CDC: community water fluoridation adjusts the fluoride in drinking water to a level recommended for preventing cavities.

evidence_cards.claim: Water fluoridation reduces cavities by about 25%
evidence_cards.snippet: CDC: drinking fluoridated water keeps teeth strong and reduces cavities by about 25% in children and adults.

evidence_cards.claim: Smoking causes lung cancer
evidence_cards.snippet: CDC: cigarette smoking causes many diseases, including cancer, heart disease, stroke and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

evidence_cards.claim: Secondhand smoke can cause lung cancer in nonsmokers
evidence_cards.snippet: CDC: in adults, secondhand smoke can cause coronary heart disease, stroke and lung cancer; it contributes to over 40,000 deaths among nonsmoking adults each year.

evidence_cards.claim: Quitting smoking lowers the risk of heart disease and cancer
evidence_cards.snippet: CDC: quitting improves health and reduces the risk of premature death and of smoking-related diseases, including heart disease, cancer and COPD.

evidence_cards.claim: Smoking only harms the lungs
evidence_cards.snippet: CDC: cigarette smoking harms nearly every organ of the body; it causes cancer, heart disease, stroke, lung diseases, type 2 diabetes and other conditions.

evidence_cards.claim: Two doses of MMR vaccine are about 97% effective against measles
evidence_cards.snippet: CDC: two doses of MMR vaccine are about 97% effective at preventing measles; one dose is about 93% effective.

evidence_cards.claim: The MMR vaccine is safe and effective
evidence_cards.snippet: CDC: MMR is safe and effective, and it provides long-lasting protection against all strains of measles.

evidence_cards.claim: Measles is not very contagious
evidence_cards.snippet: CDC: measles is highly contagious; if one person has it, up to 9 out of 10 nearby people will become infected if they are not protected.

evidence_cards.claim: Aspartame and other artificial sweeteners cause cancer in people
evidence_cards.snippet: NCI: studies reviewed by the FDA showed no evidence that approved artificial sweeteners cause cancer or other harms in people.

evidence_cards.claim: Cell phones cause brain cancer
evidence_cards.source_name: NCI · Cell phones and cancer risk
evidence_cards.snippet: NCI: the evidence to date suggests that cell phone use does not cause brain or other kinds of cancer in humans.

evidence_cards.claim: Antibiotics cannot cause serious infections
evidence_cards.snippet: CDC: serious side effects of antibiotics include C. diff infection, which causes diarrhea that can lead to severe colon damage and death.

demo_inputs.label: Both refuted
demo_inputs.text: Getting a flu vaccine gives you the flu, and antibiotics can treat a common cold.

demo_inputs.label: Mixed three states
demo_inputs.text: You must drink eight glasses of water a day or you will get sick; besides, the Earth is round.

demo_inputs.label: Refusal with no evidence
demo_inputs.text: A certain water purifier can cure diabetes, and drinking water can make you ten centimetres taller in a week.

demo_inputs.label: Coverage showcase
demo_inputs.text: Microwave ovens make food radioactive, and humans use only ten percent of their brains.

demo_inputs.label: Paraphrase robustness
demo_inputs.text: The flu vaccine contains live virus and causes infection, and the Earth is round.

demo_inputs.label: New coverage: cancer, MSG, vision
demo_inputs.text: Eating sugar makes cancer worse, MSG is harmful to health, and eating carrots supports eye health.

demo_inputs.label: Comma-separated enumeration
demo_inputs.text: Mobile-phone radiation causes cancer, an alkaline diet can cure cancer.

demo_inputs.label: Two atoms that cannot both be true
demo_inputs.text: The Earth is round and the Earth is flat.

demo_inputs.label: A two-step chain that contradicts itself
demo_inputs.text: Coffee causes cancer. Cancer causes death. Coffee prevents death.
